summary: Updates the security considerations for the MD5 message digest algorithm and for HMAC-MD5, reflecting what is known about their weaknesses. It updates RFC 1321 and RFC 2104. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6151 updates security advice for MD5 and HMAC-MD5. It says MD5 must not be used when a system needs protection against two different messages having the same digest, and new protocol designs should choose another message-authentication method instead of HMAC-MD5.

questions: what does rfc 6151 say about hmac-md5
subtitle: Updated guidance says where MD5 is no longer acceptable and why new designs should avoid HMAC-MD5.

tldr.problem: Published attacks have weakened confidence in MD5, while earlier RFCs contained security guidance that needed updating.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6151 replaces the security considerations in the MD5 specification and updates the HMAC security considerations using the attacks and analyses described in the memo.
tldr.outcome: MD5 is not acceptable when collision resistance is needed, such as for digital signatures. The memo does not call for urgently removing HMAC-MD5 from existing protocols, but says new protocol designs should not include it.

today: RFC 6151 is Informational and updates RFC 1321 and RFC 2104. Its guidance is that MD5 is not acceptable where collision resistance is required and new designs should not use HMAC-MD5.

sections.title: What the Update Covers
sections.content:
MD5 takes a message of any length and produces a 128-bit message digest. RFC 6151 replaces the security considerations in RFC 1321, which defines MD5, and updates the security considerations for HMAC in RFC 2104.

The RFC distinguishes security uses from an inline MD5 checksum used only to detect accidental errors. It says that use remains acceptable, but applications and protocols must state what security service they expect from MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 turns data into a 128-bit digest. This RFC updates its security advice and says a protocol must be clear about what protection it expects from MD5.

sections.title: Collision and Pre-Image Attacks
sections.content:
A collision occurs when two different messages produce the same digest. The RFC summarizes attacks that made MD5 collisions practical, including a cited result that found a collision in about one minute on a standard notebook computer. It also notes that MD5 collision attacks had been applied to X.509 certificates.

The cited pre-image results were much less effective. The best result described in the RFC had complexity 2^123.4, which the authors considered still high. The main warning follows from the collision attacks: MD5 is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Researchers found practical ways to create different messages with the same MD5 digest. That makes MD5 unsuitable when a digest must prove that a message is unique, such as in a digital signature.

sections.title: What the RFC Says About HMAC-MD5
sections.content:
HMAC uses a secret key together with a hash function to authenticate messages. The RFC reviews attacks on constructions related to HMAC-MD5 and a distinguishing attack on HMAC-MD5. It says the attacks do not appear to show a practical vulnerability when HMAC-MD5 is used as a message authentication code.

The effect of the distinguishing attack when HMAC is used as a pseudorandom function, such as in key derivation, is not well understood in the RFC. The authors therefore say it may not be urgent to remove HMAC-MD5 from existing protocols, while advising against including it in new designs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not say that HMAC-MD5 must immediately be removed from existing systems. It says the available attacks do not appear practical for message authentication, but the effect in key derivation is not well understood.

sections.title: Recommended Alternatives
sections.content:
The RFC says MD5 must not be used where collision resistance is required, including digital signatures. Since new protocol designs should not employ HMAC-MD5, it names HMAC-SHA256 as an alternative and also names AES-CMAC when AES is more readily available than a hash function.

These recommendations are the security guidance in this Informational update. They do not change the MD5 or HMAC message formats; RFC 6151 updates the security considerations associated with the earlier specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not choose MD5 for digital signatures or other tasks that require collision resistance. For a new design, the RFC points to HMAC-SHA256 or, in some settings, AES-CMAC.
